newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urged to deny nuclear certification to China.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urged to deny nuclear certification to China.

text.p: President Bill Clinton should not certify a nuclear cooperation agreement with China because China has failed to adopt export controls to halt the proliferation of nuclear weapons to countries such as Iran, a group of bipartisan members of Congress said on Thursday.
The certification of a 1985 nuclear cooperation agreement is required before U.S. firms can sell nuclear power plants or fissile materials to China.
A letter to Clinton from 62 members of Congress objected to certification because of fears materials sold to China might get into the wrong hands.
"We do not believe that there exists substantial evidence that China has adopted export controls that are effective at halting the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," the letter said.
"We are concerned that certifying the 1985 Nuclear Cooperation Agreement could accelerate the acquisition of nuclear weapons by non-weapons states such as Pakistan or Iran," it said.

Although the bilateral agreement was signed in 1985, no president has been able to certify that China has halted all exports of nuclear technology to nations with unsafeguarded nuclear facilities to ensure that nuclear material does not fall into the hands of non-weapons states, the letter said.

Last year China reportedly sold 5,000 ring magnets to Pakistan for use in Pakistan's uranium enrichment facility, the letter said. Both Pakistan and China denied that the sale occurred, and the Clinton administration decided not to impose sanctions in exchange for China's assurance that it would safeguard its nuclear facilities.
The certification is supported by nuclear power reactor manufacturers in the United States, where no new nuclear power plants have been built in a generation.

The U.S. industry said earlier this year it hoped the president would certify the agreement, clearing the way for sales to China by early 1998. The U.S. companies are focusing on China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea as promising markets for their new technology.
The letter was signed by Democratic Representative Edward Markey of Massachusetts, Republican Representative Gerald Solomon of New York and 60 other members of Congress.
